title: Tiredness in an Adolescent - Grief Reaction
patient_instructions: You play BOTH roles as directed by the candidate. As the MOTHER (Karen): you are worried about your 14-year-old daughter Emily, who has been tired for about two months. You are anxious, protective and keen for blood tests. Volunteer that she 'used to be a great student but her grades have dropped in the last couple of months' if asked about school/function. If asked directly, mention that your mother (Emily's grandmother, whom she was very close to) died four months ago. You are unsure about sensitive topics and would say 'I don't think so' if asked whether Emily is sexually active - but a good candidate should offer to speak with Emily alone. As EMILY (14, if the candidate interviews you alone with confidentiality explained): you feel flat and tired, miss your grandmother a lot, sometimes cry at night and find it hard to concentrate at school. You are not using drugs or alcohol, are not sexually active, have no weight loss, fevers or night sweats. If gently asked about self-harm, say you have felt 'what's the point' occasionally but have no plan and would never act on it, and you still enjoy seeing your best friend. Affect: subdued, quiet, opens up if the candidate is warm and non-judgemental.
candidate_instructions: You are a GP at a rural NSW practice. Karen has brought her 14-year-old daughter Emily because Emily has been 'tired all the time' for two months. In 8 minutes: take a focused history exploring the fatigue and its impact, screen the key differentials, appropriately assess this adolescent (including offering to see her alone), request a focused examination from the examiner, and explain your most likely diagnosis and initial management plan to the family.
examiner_instructions: This is a psychosocial 'pitfall' variant of the tiredness cluster - the answer is a grief reaction presenting somatically. Reward candidates who: explore tiredness (energy/sleep/fever, timing, functional and school impact); screen organic causes (endocrine, malignancy, infection/post-viral, anaemia, coeliac, OSA); and crucially recognise the need to interview the adolescent ALONE with confidentiality explained (HEEADSSS) and perform a mood/suicide risk assessment given recent bereavement. On examination reveal normal vitals, a small (<1 cm) soft mobile reactive cervical node, no hepatosplenomegaly, normal BSL/urinalysis. The candidate should reassure about the benign node, diagnose grief reaction, list differentials (MDD, PTSD, post-viral, leukaemia) and arrange baseline bloods, grief/bereavement support, school liaison and safety-net follow-up. Prompt if needed: 'Is there anyone else you would want to speak to?'

criteria: Introduces self, gains cooperation and explores what 'tired' means (energy, sleep, fever, timing)
Assesses functional and school-performance impact (grades dropping over two months)
Offers to interview the adolescent ALONE and explains confidentiality and its limits (HEEADSSS)
Elicits the significant bereavement (grandmother died 4 months ago) and psychosocial stressors
Screens sensitive topics (mood, drugs, sexual activity) directly with the young person rather than by proxy
Screens organic differentials (endocrine, infection/post-viral, anaemia, coeliac, OSA, malignancy)
Requests focused examination (general appearance, vitals, thyroid, lymph nodes, hepatosplenomegaly, BSL/urinalysis)
Interprets the cervical node as benign/reactive (<1 cm, soft, mobile) and not concerning
Identifies grief reaction as most likely, with MDD, PTSD, post-viral fatigue and leukaemia as differentials
Performs an explicit mood and suicide/self-harm risk assessment (thoughts, plan, protective factors)
Recognises persistent functional impairment at 4 months warrants active follow-up, not pure reassurance (prolonged grief/adjustment disorder framing)
Arranges first-line paediatric fatigue bloods (FBE/film, iron studies, TSH, EBV serology, coeliac serology)
Provides grief counselling/bereavement support, school liaison, family involvement and a safety-net review
Warm, non-judgemental, developmentally appropriate communication with mother and adolescent
Explains diagnosis and plan in plain language and checks understanding

red_flags: Suicidal ideation, hopelessness or self-harm in a bereaved adolescent with functional decline (recent bereavement is a recognised risk factor)

Fixed, hard, matted or supraclavicular lymph nodes >1 cm, drenching night sweats, hepatosplenomegaly, unexplained bruising/petechiae or pallor - features of leukaemia/lymphoma requiring urgent FBE/film and paediatric referral
Unintentional weight loss and persistent fever suggesting malignancy or serious infection
Prolonged functional impairment beyond expected grief timeline suggesting major depressive disorder or prolonged grief disorder
australian_guidelines: RACGP adolescent health / HEEADSSS psychosocial assessment: offer confidential time alone with the young person, explain confidentiality and its limits, and explore sensitive topics directly (respecting Gillick/mature-minor competence)

RACGP/beyondblue guidance: any adolescent with functional decline and a significant loss must be screened for depression and suicidality (mood, hopelessness, thoughts of self-harm, plan, protective factors)
DSM-5-TR / ICD-11: distinguish normal grief from prolonged grief disorder and adjustment disorder using a timeline - persistent impairment at 4 months warrants active follow-up
eTG / RACGP paediatric fatigue work-up: first-line FBE and film, iron studies, TSH, EBV serology/monospot and coeliac serology, with paediatric referral if red flags
Murtagh: bereavement counselling is a defined GP task with structured guidance
learning_objectives: Recognise that grief and mood disorders in young people often present with somatic symptoms such as tiredness and falling school performance
Conduct a confidential, developmentally appropriate adolescent interview using HEEADSSS
Perform a structured mood and suicide risk assessment in a bereaved young person
Differentiate normal grief from major depression, adjustment disorder and prolonged grief disorder
Order appropriate first-line investigations and safety-net a fatigue presentation while excluding malignancy red flags
key_points: Never take an adolescent's psychosocial and sexual history by proxy from a parent - offer time alone with confidentiality explained
Recent bereavement plus functional decline mandates an explicit suicide risk assessment
A small (<1 cm), soft, mobile cervical node is reactive and reassuring; fixed/hard/supraclavicular nodes are red flags
Persistent impairment at 4 months is beyond typical uncomplicated grief and needs active follow-up
Management is holistic: bereavement support, school liaison, family involvement and baseline bloods to exclude organic causes

citations.claim: Bereavement counselling is a defined GP task with structured guidance in Murtagh, supporting management of a grief reaction.
citations.source: John Murtagh General Practice, 8th Edition.pdf, p.3553 (counselling for bereavement pp.29-30)

citations.claim: Recent bereavement is listed as a risk factor for depression and suicide, reinforcing the need for a mood/risk assessment.
citations.source: John Murtagh General Practice, 8th Edition.pdf, p.3353

citations.claim: Hypothyroidism (tiredness/lethargy, cold intolerance, weight gain) is a legitimate endocrine differential to screen for in fatigue.
citations.source: John Murtagh General Practice, 8th Edition.pdf, p.352
